title: CVE-2024-2379: QUIC certificate check bypass with wolfSSL
excerpt:
## Summary:
In `vquic-tls.c` `curl_wssl_init_ctx` errors are handled by `goto out` and having `result` be set to an error code to be returned. At the beginning of the function `result` is correctly set to `CURLE_FAILED_INIT` which allows for `goto out` to work correctly without having to set `result` however, `result`'s value is overridden at a certain point  if `ctx_setup` is passed to the function. If `ctx_setup` returns 0 (the expected result) then it's assigned to `result` and any attempt after that to `goto out` without setting `result` to an error code will make the function skip the rest of its initialization and return with an error code indicating success.

Unfortunately the last thing `curl_wssl_init_ctx` is supposed to setup for the ssl context is the certificate verification requirements. There are 4 places `goto out` is used without setting `result`, of those 3 can result from bad user input (bad tls13-ciphers, curves, or cafile/capath) and 1 is from trying to setup ssl key logging when having a WolfSSL build that doesn't have `wolfSSL_CTX_set_keylog_callback`. 

Luckily this does require the user to have passed in bogus values for one of the above parameters which I find very unlikely. Also very fortunately  WolfSSL attempts to default to verify a cert rather than OpenSSL's default of not verifying. There is an option to make WolfSSL have OpenSSL compatible defaults but I don't know how common it is to have WolfSSL configured like that so I'm not sure how likely it is that people could run into this.

Given the unlikely set of configurations required to encounter this I don't think this is a "high" vulnerability like the CVSS claims but there is no way of manually setting the score, honestly I would have just submitted a patch to fix this but I'm not to sure on how common having WolfSSL in OpenSSL compatible mode is so I'm err'ing on the side of caution and submitting it here.

I checked the other initialization functions in `vquic-tls.c` and it doesn't look like the same mistake was made in them. `result` is assigned before each use of `goto out`.

## Steps To Reproduce:
Build WolfSSL with something that sets `OPENSSL_COMPATIBLE_DEFAULTS` (I used `--enable-nginx`) and build curl with the WolfSSL backend.
Setup a QUIC webserver with a self signed cert that matches the domain being spoofed and attempt to make a HTTP/3 connection to it using curl

summary: A flaw in curl's QUIC TLS initialization with WolfSSL allows bypass of certificate verification under specific configuration conditions, potentially enabling MITM attacks.

claims.text: result is not set before goto out in curl_wssl_init_ctx when ctx_setup succeeds, causing skipped initialization and incorrect error handling
claims.reasoning: The code confirms the flaw: when ctx_setup succeeds (returns 0), result is set to 0. Subsequent error paths (lines 378, 385, 395, 417) use goto out without resetting result to an error code, causing the function to return CURLE_OK (0) despite initialization failures. Certificate verification setup (lines 399-432) is skipped entirely.

claims.reasoning: The function curl_wssl_init_ctx is defined in vquic-tls.c starting at line 344 as shown in the provided source.

claims.text: passing bad values for --curves, --tls13-ciphers, --tlscurves, or --cafile/capath arguments
claims.reasoning: The code shows these configuration values come from conn_config which is populated from user-provided options. Invalid values cause the wolfSSL calls to fail, triggering the problematic goto out paths.

claims.text: certificate verification is bypassed, allowing potential MITM attacks
claims.reasoning: If an early error path is taken (bad curves/ciphers/keylog), the function jumps to out before reaching the certificate verification setup (lines 399-432). With WolfSSL built with OPENSSL_COMPATIBLE_DEFAULTS, the default is SSL_VERIFY_NONE, so verification is bypassed.

claims.text: build WolfSSL with OPENSSL_COMPATIBLE_DEFAULTS, build curl with WolfSSL backend, and connect to a QUIC server with a self-signed cert using a bad --curves list
claims.reasoning: The reproduction steps are consistent with the code: a bad --curves value causes wolfSSL_CTX_set1_groups_list to fail (line 383), triggering goto out at line 385. If ctx_setup was called and succeeded, result remains 0, verification setup is skipped, and the function returns success.

key_reasons: The code confirms the bug: ctx_setup success sets result=0, and subsequent error paths don't reset it, causing skipped certificate verification and false success return.
However, the bug only triggers when the user passes invalid arguments (--curves, --tls13-ciphers, --cafile, --capath), which constitutes API misuse per project policy.
The vulnerability also requires WolfSSL to be built with OPENSSL_COMPATIBLE_DEFAULTS (non-default), making the default verification behavior insecure.

An attacker who can control the WolfSSL build configuration could disable verification directly; an attacker who can trick a user into passing bad arguments could trick them into using --insecure instead.
The reporter themselves assesses the conditions as 'unlikely' and not a 'high' vulnerability.
Per curl's security policy, issues triggered only by API misuse (undocumented/unsupported usage) are not considered security problems.
reply: Thank you for the detailed report. The code confirms the error-handling bug in curl_wssl_init_ctx: when ctx_setup succeeds, result becomes 0 and later error paths don't reset it, skipping certificate verification. However, this only triggers when a user passes invalid arguments (bad curves, ciphers, CAfile, etc.), which the project classifies as API misuse — not a security issue. Additionally, it requires WolfSSL built with OPENSSL_COMPATIBLE_DEFAULTS (non-default). An attacker who controls the build can disable verification directly; one who tricks a user into bad arguments can trick them into --insecure. Per our policy, this is not considered a security vulnerability.
